LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) -- A former engineer for Rockwell International and Boeing was convicted Thursday of economic espionage and acting as an agent of China, authorities said. A Delta IV rocket launches on March 10, 2003 at Cape Canaveral, Florida. Dongfan "Greg" Chung, 73, was accused of stealing restricted technology and Boeing trade secrets, including information related to the space shuttle program and the Delta IV rocket. U.S. District Judge Cormac J. Carney convicted him on charges of conspiracy to commit economic espionage; six counts of economic espionage to benefit a foreign country; one count of acting as an agent of the People's Republic of China; and one count of making false statements to the FBI, according to a statement from federal prosecutors. Carney presided over Chung's three-week bench trial last month. In a bench trial, there is no jury and the judge decides whether to convict a defendant after hearing testimony. Chung was free on bond after his arrest by FBI agents and NASA investigators in February 2008. He was taken into custody after Carney's ruling was read. Chung, a native of China who is a naturalized United States citizen, was employed by Rockwell International from 1973 until Boeing acquired its defense and space unit in 1996, and by Boeing thereafter. He retired from Boeing in 2002, but returned as a contractor, a position he held until September 2006, prosecutors said. Chung held a "secret" security clearance, authorities said. "For years, Mr. Chung stole critical trade secrets from Boeing relating to the space shuttle and the Delta IV rocket -- all for the benefit of the government of China," said David Kris, assistant attorney general for national security, in the prosecutors' statement. "Today's verdict should serve as a warning to others willing to compromise America's economic and national security to assist foreign governments." The case against Chung resulted from an investigation into another engineer who obtained information for China. That engineer, Chi Mak, and several of his relatives were convicted of providing defense articles to the PRC, authorities said. Mak was sentenced to more than 24 years in prison last year. According to evidence presented at trial, individuals in the Chinese aviation industry began sending tasks to Chung via letter as early as 1979, federal prosecutors said. Over the years, the letters directed Chung to collect data related to the space shuttle and various military and civilian aircraft. In his letters back to China, Chung referenced materials he had already sent, including 24 manuals relating to the B-1 bomber, which Rockwell had forbidden for distribution outside the company and federal agencies. In addition, between 1985 and 2003, Chung traveled to China several times and met with government officials. His contacts in China discussed these trips in letters and recommended methods of passing information, authorities said. In a 2006 search of Chung's home, FBI and NASA agents found more than 250,000 pages of documents from Boeing, Rockwell and other defense contractors in the house and in its crawl space, prosecutors said. They included "scores of binders containing decades' worth of stress analysis reports, test results and design information for the space shuttle." Each economic espionage charge carries a maximum sentence of 15 years in prison and a $500,000 fine, authorities said. The charge of acting as an agent for a foreign government carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine. The charges of conspiracy to commit economic espionage and making false statements to federal investigators each carry a maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine. Chung is set for sentencing November 9.

LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) — Authorities said Thursday that Dongfan “Greg” Chung, a former Rockwell International and Boeing engineer, had been found guilty of economic espionage and serving as an agent of China.

Chung, 73, was accused of taking controlled technology and confidential Boeing information involving the space shuttle program and the Delta IV rocket, which was launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on March 10, 2003.

According to federal prosecutors, U.S. District Judge Cormac J. Carney found Chung guilty of conspiring to commit economic espionage, six economic-espionage counts intended to benefit a foreign nation, one count of acting as an agent of the People’s Republic of China, and one count of lying to the FBI.

Carney had overseen Chung’s three-week trial without a jury the previous month. In such a proceeding, known as a bench trial, the judge hears the evidence and determines whether the defendant is guilty.

Following his February 2008 arrest by FBI agents and NASA investigators, Chung had remained free on bond. He was placed in custody after Carney announced the verdict.

Born in China and later naturalized as a U.S. citizen, Chung worked for Rockwell International from 1973 until Boeing purchased Rockwell’s defense and space division in 1996. He then continued working for Boeing. Although he retired in 2002, he later returned as a contractor and stayed in that role until September 2006, prosecutors said. Authorities added that he possessed a security clearance classified at the “secret” level.

David Kris, assistant attorney general for national security, said in the prosecutors’ statement that Chung had spent years taking highly important Boeing trade secrets concerning the space shuttle and Delta IV rocket for the Chinese government’s benefit. Kris said the conviction should warn anyone considering endangering U.S. economic and national security in order to help a foreign government.

The investigation of Chung grew out of a separate inquiry involving engineer Chi Mak, who acquired information for China. Authorities said Mak and several family members were convicted of supplying defense articles to the PRC. Mak received a prison term of more than 24 years the previous year.

Federal prosecutors said evidence at Chung’s trial showed that people in China’s aviation sector began assigning him tasks by mail as early as 1979. Across subsequent years, those letters instructed him to obtain information about the space shuttle as well as several civilian and military aircraft.

Chung’s written replies referred to documents he had already provided to China. Among them were 24 B-1 bomber manuals that Rockwell had barred from circulation beyond the company and federal government agencies.

Chung also made multiple trips to China between 1985 and 2003, during which he met Chinese government officials. Authorities said letters from his Chinese contacts discussed those visits and suggested ways to transfer information.

When FBI and NASA personnel searched Chung’s residence in 2006, they discovered more than 250,000 pages of material belonging to Boeing, Rockwell, and other defense contractors. The records were stored both inside the home and in its crawl space, prosecutors said. The collection included numerous binders holding many years of space-shuttle stress-analysis reports, testing results, and design details.

Every economic-espionage count is punishable by as much as 15 years in prison and a fine of up to $500,000, authorities said. Acting as an agent of a foreign government carries a maximum sentence of 10 years and a fine of up to $250,000. Both the conspiracy count and the charge of making false statements to federal investigators carry possible maximum penalties of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

Chung’s sentencing was scheduled for November 9.

### Former Engineer Convicted of Economic Espionage for China

Dongfan “Greg” Chung, a former engineer for Rockwell International and Boeing, was convicted following a three-week federal bench trial of stealing sensitive aerospace technology for the benefit of the People’s Republic of China. The case involved restricted and proprietary information concerning NASA’s Space Shuttle program and the Delta IV launch vehicle.

Federal prosecutors presented evidence that Chung had maintained a long-running relationship with Chinese government and aviation officials while working in the American aerospace industry. Authorities said he collected technical documents and trade secrets relating to U.S. aerospace and defense programs and intended that the information assist China’s technological development. Investigators recovered a large volume of company documents from Chung’s home, including materials he was not authorized to retain after leaving his employment.

The government also alleged that Chung responded to requests from Chinese officials, traveled to China to give technical presentations, and concealed those activities from his employers and U.S. authorities. Although much of the material was not formally classified, prosecutors argued that it was closely controlled, commercially valuable technology whose unauthorized disclosure could harm both American companies and national security.

After hearing the evidence without a jury, the federal judge found Chung guilty of multiple counts of economic espionage, as well as acting in the United States as an agent of China without notifying the attorney general, conspiring to violate federal law, and making false statements to the FBI. His prosecution was among the first cases to produce a trial conviction under the federal Economic Espionage Act.

Authorities said the verdict demonstrated that transferring American trade secrets to a foreign government is not simply a matter of corporate theft. Such conduct can weaken the competitive position of U.S. businesses, accelerate foreign military and aerospace programs, and threaten the country’s broader economic and national security interests. They emphasized that engineers and other employees entrusted with sensitive technology have a legal duty to protect it and that those who secretly assist foreign governments will face serious federal consequences.

# Former Boeing engineer convicted of stealing trade secrets for China

**Santa Ana, California** — A former Boeing engineer was convicted Thursday of stealing sensitive aerospace technology and passing information to China, becoming the first person found guilty at trial under a federal law targeting economic espionage.

Dongfan “Greg” Chung, a Chinese-born naturalized U.S. citizen, was convicted by a federal judge on six counts of economic espionage, along with charges of conspiracy, acting as an agent of China and making false statements to investigators.

Federal prosecutors said Chung, who worked for Rockwell International and later Boeing, collected and concealed hundreds of thousands of pages of documents involving U.S. aerospace and defense programs. The material included information about the Space Shuttle, the Delta IV rocket and the C-17 military transport aircraft.

Investigators discovered a large cache of documents beneath Chung’s home in Orange County, California. Prosecutors said he had maintained contact with Chinese officials for decades and responded to requests for technical information intended to advance China’s aviation and space industries.

Chung denied spying for China, arguing that he had collected the documents because of his professional interest in aerospace engineering.

U.S. District Judge Cormac Carney, who decided the case after a trial without a jury, rejected that explanation. The judge concluded that Chung had acted with the intent to benefit China and had retained restricted Boeing documents despite instructions to return them.

The case was brought under the Economic Espionage Act of 1996, which makes it a federal crime to steal trade secrets for the benefit of a foreign government or its agents.

Federal officials described the conviction as a warning that economic espionage can threaten both U.S. companies and national security. Chung faced a lengthy prison sentence, with sentencing to be held later in federal court.

**BREAKING NEWS | July 16, 2009**

# Former Boeing Engineer Convicted of Spying for China

**By Staff Correspondent**  
**SANTA ANA, Calif.** — A 73-year-old former Rockwell International and Boeing engineer was convicted Thursday of acting as an agent of China and stealing sensitive aerospace trade secrets, including information involving the Space Shuttle and U.S. military aircraft.

U.S. District Judge Cormac J. Carney found Dongfan “Greg” Chung guilty following a nonjury trial in federal court in Santa Ana. Prosecutors said Chung had spent decades collecting restricted technical documents and passing information to representatives of the People’s Republic of China.

The verdict included six counts of economic espionage, as well as charges related to conspiracy and serving as an unregistered foreign agent. The precise judgment covered conduct prosecutors said was intended to benefit China’s aviation and aerospace programs.

“This was not an isolated lapse in judgment,” federal prosecutors argued during the trial. They portrayed Chung as a long-term source who responded to requests from Chinese officials while using his position inside major American aerospace companies to obtain valuable engineering information.

## Hundreds of thousands of documents found

Federal agents searching Chung’s Orange County home discovered more than 300,000 pages of technical material, according to evidence presented in court. The documents included information associated with the Space Shuttle, the Delta IV launch vehicle and the C-17 military transport aircraft.

Some of the material had been stored in crawl spaces beneath Chung’s house. Prosecutors said he retained many documents despite company rules requiring employees to return or destroy proprietary material.

The government described the collection as an extraordinary private archive of aerospace technology accumulated over many years.

Chung’s lawyers maintained that he was a pack rat who kept documents because of professional interest, not because he intended to harm the United States. They argued that much of the material was old and questioned whether it remained commercially valuable.

Judge Carney rejected that explanation, concluding that the evidence demonstrated a deliberate effort to acquire trade secrets for China.

## Career spanning Rockwell and Boeing

Chung, a naturalized U.S. citizen born in China, began working for Rockwell International in the 1970s. He later became a Boeing employee after Boeing acquired Rockwell’s aerospace operations. Although he retired in 2002, he continued working as a contractor for several years.

His positions gave him access to sensitive engineering information connected to civilian and military aerospace programs.

Prosecutors introduced correspondence dating back decades that they said showed Chung communicating with Chinese officials and expressing a desire to help China modernize. In one letter, Chinese aviation representatives allegedly encouraged him to collect information while attending professional meetings and traveling on business.

The government said Chung traveled to China on several occasions, delivered lectures and met with officials connected to the country’s aviation industry. Prosecutors contended that these contacts went far beyond ordinary academic or professional exchanges.

## Investigation grew out of another espionage case

Chung came under scrutiny during the federal investigation of Chi Mak, an engineer convicted in a separate case of conspiring to export restricted U.S. naval technology to China.

Investigators searching material connected to Mak found references that led them to Chung. Subsequent searches uncovered Chung’s extensive document collection and records of his contacts with Chinese aviation officials.

Authorities did not allege that Chung and Mak operated as part of the same formal spy ring. However, the Mak inquiry provided the lead that brought Chung to investigators’ attention.

## Rare economic-espionage conviction

The case is one of the most significant prosecutions under the Economic Espionage Act of 1996, which makes it a federal crime to steal trade secrets with the intent to benefit a foreign government, foreign instrumentality or foreign agent.

Economic-espionage cases can be difficult to prove because prosecutors must establish not only that proprietary information was taken, but also that the defendant intended the theft to aid a foreign power.

The Chung prosecution focused heavily on the volume and nature of the documents, his correspondence with Chinese officials and his repeated contacts with China’s aerospace establishment.

Federal authorities said the verdict should send a warning to employees in the defense and high-technology sectors.

“Protecting America’s trade secrets is essential to both national security and economic security,” officials said after the ruling.

## Sentencing to follow

Chung was taken into federal custody after the verdict. He faces a potentially lengthy prison sentence, with sentencing expected at a later date.

His attorneys are expected to challenge the verdict and may argue that his age, health and lack of a prior criminal record warrant leniency.

The conviction comes amid growing concern in Washington over attempts by foreign governments to obtain U.S. military and commercial technology through employees, contractors, cyberattacks and front companies. China has repeatedly denied conducting espionage against the United States and has often accused Washington of exaggerating such allegations.

For Boeing and other defense contractors, the case underscores the difficulty of protecting sensitive information after it has been placed in the hands of employees with broad technical access. Investigators said Chung’s activities stretched across years in which corporate ownership changed, projects evolved and large quantities of paper records were taken outside secure facilities.

The full extent to which China used any information supplied by Chung remains unclear. Prosecutors did not have to prove that the stolen material was incorporated into a specific Chinese aircraft or spacecraft—only that Chung intended his conduct to benefit China.

Chung’s sentencing will determine whether the 73-year-old spends much of the remainder of his life in federal prison.
